result.summary: Apollo reveals himself to Achilles, who then turns on Hector waiting outside Troy's walls. After Priam and Hecuba fail to move him, Hector flees three times around the city, is tricked by Minerva, and is killed by Achilles, who drags his body behind his chariot while Troy, and Andromache, mourn.

scenes.title: Apollo Reveals Himself
scenes.summary: Apollo tells Achilles he cannot be killed, and Achilles angrily blames him for saving the Trojans before turning toward the city.
scenes.stakes: Achilles risks losing glory and revenge on the Trojans.

place.name: before Ilius and the Scaean gates

scenes.title: Priam and Hecuba Plead
scenes.summary: Priam and Hecuba beg Hector from the wall to come inside, but he stands firm.
scenes.stakes: Priam and Hecuba stand to lose their son, and Priam fears a shameful death.

scenes.title: Hector's Doubts and Flight
scenes.summary: Hector debates yielding, then fears Achilles and flees. They race three times around the city past the springs of Scamander.

scenes.title: The Gods Decide
scenes.summary: Jove, pitying Hector, lets Minerva intervene. Jove weighs the dooms in his golden scales and Hector's sinks, so Apollo leaves him.
scenes.stakes: Hector's fate is decided by the gods.

place.name: Olympus and the plain of Troy

scenes.title: Minerva's Trick and Hector's Death
scenes.summary: Minerva, disguised as Deiphobus, persuades Hector to stand. After spears are thrown, Hector charges with his sword and Achilles kills him, refusing ransom.
scenes.stakes: Hector's life; Achilles' vengeance for Patroclus.

scenes.title: Desecration of the Body
scenes.summary: The Achaeans stab Hector's corpse. Achilles speaks of Patroclus, pierces the feet and drags the body behind his chariot.

scenes.title: Troy Laments
scenes.summary: Priam and Hecuba cry out in grief as the city wails and Priam begs to go to the ships.
scenes.stakes: Priam's grief and the city's loss of its defender.

scenes.title: Andromache's Lament
scenes.summary: Hector's wife, unaware, prepares a bath, hears the cries, rushes to the wall and faints at the sight. She mourns Hector and foresees the fate of their son Astyanax.
scenes.stakes: Her husband is dead; her son faces destitution.

alias_notes.explanation: Pallas is a title of Minerva (Athena).

notable_quotes.reason: Hector resolves to die greatly, so that it is remembered.
Achilles rejects Hector's pact with a lions-and-men image.
Jove's golden scales settle Hector's fate.

analysis.text: Fate and divine will govern the duel, and Hector faces death with courage after deception by a god.
Achilles' rage and refusal of mercy contrast with the grief of Hector's family, preparing for Book 24.

legacy.text: The three laps round Troy and the dragging of Hector's body became a favourite subject of ancient and later art and literature.
The film Troy (2004) stages the duel of Achilles and Hector before the walls.

fun_facts.text: The weighing of fates in golden scales (kerostasia) was also used in Aeschylus' lost play Psychostasia.

language_notes.text: Apollo points out the gap between mortal and immortal: Achilles has been chasing him, disguised as a Trojan, across the plain.
Far-Darter is an epithet of Apollo, the archer god whose arrows strike from afar.
"Bitten the dust" means fallen dead in battle; "ere" means before.
Orion's Hound is the star Sirius, whose late-summer rising was linked with heat, fever and disease.
"Reft" is an archaic past form of "reave": taken away by force.
"Son of Saturn" is Jove (the Greek Zeus), son of Saturn (Cronus).
Polydamas had advised retreating into Troy the night Achilles returned to battle; Hector refused. Hector now recalls that rejected advice.
Helen's abduction by Alexandrus (Paris) caused the war. Hector imagines offering her back plus Paris's treasure and half the city's wealth.
Alludes to lovers' idle talk by a rock or oak; Hector means this is no time for gentle, trifling conversation.
"Vouchsafe" means to grant graciously; here Jove decides who wins.
"Pelian ash" refers to the spear made from ash wood of Mount Pelion, given to Peleus, Achilles' father.
"Waggon-road" is the cart track beside the wall; the "look-out station" was a watch-post on the fortifications.
Funeral games for a dead hero offered prizes like tripods and women; this recalls such contests, as in Book 23.
"Sire of gods and men" is a formulaic title for Jove, the father and ruler of the gods.
Burning thigh-bones wrapped in fat was the standard Greek sacrifice; Hector's piety is why Jove feels he deserves help.
"Trito-born" is an epithet of Minerva (the Greek Athena), of uncertain origin, often linked to Lake Triton.
"Without let or hindrance" means without any obstruction or restraint; "let" here means hindrance.
"Dardanian gates" are the gates of Troy, named for Dardanus, the ancestor of the Trojan royal line.
Jove's golden scales weigh the fates of two men; the pan that sinks marks the one doomed to die.
Apollo has been protecting Hector; Minerva says even his pleading with Jove will not save him. Jove's aegis is a divine goatskin shield or cape.
"Inveigle" means to trick or lure by deceit. Minerva persuades Hector with a false appearance and false words.
"Vouchsafes" means grants graciously. Hector asks for a mutual oath that the winner will return the loser's body.
Mars is the god of war (the Greek Ares). To "glut" him with blood means to satisfy his hunger for killing.
Vulcan (the Greek Hephaestus), god of the forge, made Achilles' new armour. Hector wore the old set, taken from Patroclus.
"Scatheless" means unharmed; "recked not" means gave no thought to; "vaunted" means boasted.
"Dues of fire" means cremation, the proper funeral rite. Being eaten by dogs would deny Hector this honour.
Hector prophesies Achilles' death at the Scaean gates, the main gate of Troy, by Paris with Apollo's help.
"Vouchsafed us to overcome" means heaven has graciously granted us the ability to defeat him.
Achilles refers to the belief that the dead in Hades' realm fade into forgetfulness; he vows his loyalty to Patroclus will outlast even that.
"Contumely" means insulting, contemptuous treatment; here, the outrage of mutilating a corpse.
"Nothing loth" means not unwilling, i.e. the horses eagerly sprang forward.
"Smirched" means soiled or defiled; here the city seems to be smoldering, as if already burning.
"Suffer me" means allow me; "single-handed" means alone.
"Bane" means a cause of ruin or destruction.
"Remained without the gates" means Hector stayed outside the city gates, alone, to face Achilles.
"Double purple web" means a purple cloth woven doubled, or a double-width fabric, decorated with flower patterns.
A tripod here is a large three-legged cauldron stood over the fire to heat bath water.
"Frontlet" is a band worn across the forehead; the "net" is a hair-covering. Together they make up a married woman's headdress.
"Gifts of wooing" are the bride-price a suitor gave the bride's family.
"Fain to die" means she was eager or ready to die.
"Erewhile" is archaic for "a short time ago" or "formerly".
Astyanax means roughly "lord of the city", so the name is tied to Hector as the city's defender.

context_notes.text: Ilius is Troy. The Scaean gates were its main gate, where Hector waits.
Lycaon was sold into slavery by Achilles and later killed by him; Priam does not yet know this.
Hecuba's gesture of baring her breast is a desperate appeal to a mother's claim on her son.
Mars (the Greek Ares) is the god of war, so the comparison makes Achilles seem war incarnate.
Springs of Scamander: Troy's river, also called Xanthus; the hot and cold springs are a famous local landmark.
The washing-troughs recall Troy's lost peacetime, sharpening the contrast with the present deadly chase.
Minerva sides with the Greeks, and Hector's death has been fated; she argues that even Jove should not overturn fate.
Apollo, a Trojan ally, has protected Hector so far; he must withdraw once fate is settled.
Hades is both the god of the dead and the underworld realm where souls go.
Deiphobus is a Trojan prince, Hector's brother. Minerva (the Greek Athena) favours the Greeks and takes his form to deceive Hector.
Achilles finds the gap in the armour Hector took from Patroclus, which was Achilles' own armour lent to his friend.
Hades is the god of the dead and also names his realm, where souls dwell as shadows.
Argives and Achaeans are both names for the Greeks besieging Troy.
Peleus is Achilles' aged father, left behind in Phthia. Priam hopes Achilles may pity a father like his own.
Hecuba is Priam's wife and Hector's mother, queen of Troy.
Minerva (the Greek Athena) had earlier tricked Hector by posing as his brother Deiphobus, which led him to stand and fight.
Thebes under Placus was a small city in the Troad, not the Greek Thebes. Achilles had sacked it and killed Eetion.
Hades is the god of the dead and the name of the underworld realm where the dead go.
Burning the clothes in place of the body was a substitute honour, since Hector's corpse cannot receive proper burial.

literary_notes.text: Achilles' speed is compared to a racehorse straining across the plain, conveying his tireless drive.
The star that brings fire and fever hints that Achilles' brilliance means death for Hector and Troy.
Priam's imagined fate, his own hounds lapping his blood, makes the appeal intensely pitiable.
Hector is likened to a poisoned, coiled serpent, showing his dangerous resolve despite his parents' pleas.
Hector's questions show him wavering, imagining impossible alternatives before reality returns.
Achilles' bronze is compared to fire and the rising sun, making him dazzling and terrible.
The falcon and cowering dove convey Achilles' predatory speed and Hector's helplessness, extending the comparison across several clauses.
The stakes are raised by comparing the prize with ordinary race prizes: here the prize is Hector's life, not an animal or hide.
Jove's pity and recollection of Hector's offerings show the gods' personal attachments to mortals and make Hector sympathetic.
Achilles is likened to a hound chasing a fawn, stressing his relentless pursuit and Hector's helpless fear.
The dream-chase image conveys the stalemate of the pursuit, where neither man can close or break the gap.
The sinking scale pan symbolizes Hector's fixed fate and ends all hope, while Apollo's departure confirms it.
Achilles compares men and lions, wolves and lambs, to show that enmity between them is natural and absolute, leaving no room for agreements.
Readers know Minerva is the cause. Hector learns only now, as the disguise falls away, that his "brother" was a lie.
Hector's charge is compared to an eagle swooping on a lamb or hare, though ironically he is the prey here.
The spear's gleam is likened to the evening star, a beautiful but ominous image that stresses imminent death.
Achilles' wish to eat Hector raw shows his savage fury and his refusal of all mercy.
The Achaeans' mocking remark shows cruelty; the once-feared Hector is now a helpless body that every man can stab.
Dust, flying dark hair and a fallen head vividly picture Hector's degradation, contrasting with his former beauty.
Troy's grief is compared to the city burning, foreshadowing its eventual destruction by fire.
Calling Hector a tower of strength presents him as the city's defensive wall, so his death leaves Troy exposed.
The audience knows Hector is dead while Andromache prepares his bath, which makes her ordinary domestic care painful.
Her eyes shrouded "as with the darkness of night" conveys her blacking out as the sight overwhelms her.
The concrete picture of the orphan tugging at cloaks and shirts draws sympathy through small, humiliating details.
The detail of the cup that moistens lips but not the palate makes the child's deprivation vivid and physical.
The worms and dogs at the ships are set against the earlier picture of Hector's fine house and clothes, sharpening the loss.
